title: Strict Value Comparison Breaks the Competitive Guarantee
body_html:
Strict Value Comparison Breaks the Competitive Guarantee

Counterexample (welfare_eq_zero). Consider the sample-then-threshold variant of the online single-item auction (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) that observes the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ arrivals, then accepts any later bidder whose value is strictly greater than the maximum value observed in the observe phase. This rule is not $1/4$-competitive, even for $n = 2$ and injective identities.

Construction

Fix any $M > 0$ and set $n = 2$, $v = (M, M)$ — two bidders with identical value $M$. The auction observes one bidder (the observe phase is $\lfloor 2/2 \rfloor = 1$ arrival long), then admits any later bidder whose value strictly exceeds the observed value.

Welfare on every permutation is zero

There are two arrival orders.

  • $\sigma = \mathrm{id}$: Bidder $0$ arrives first and is rejected during the observe phase. The observed maximum is $M$. Bidder $1$ arrives with value $M$; the strict test $M > M$ fails, so bidder $1$ is also rejected. Welfare $= 0$.
  • $\sigma = (0\;1)$: Bidder $1$ arrives first (rejected). Observed maximum is again $M$. Bidder $0$ arrives with value $M$; $M > M$ fails. Welfare $= 0$.

The bound is violated

$$ \frac{1}{2!}\sum_{\sigma} \mathrm{welfare}(\sigma) = 0 \;<\; \frac{1}{4} \cdot M = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\max_i v_i. $$

Remarks

Why it fails

Strict value comparison cannot distinguish between the observed bidder and a later bidder with the same value. In the sample-then-threshold skeleton the threshold is set to the maximum observed value; any later bidder whose value equals this maximum is "as good as the best seen so far" and should be accepted, but strict comparison rejects them.

The single-item auction's acceptance rule (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) resolves this by attaching an identity tag to the threshold: at exactly the threshold price, the bidder's identity has to clear an identity tag as well. In the sample-then-threshold auction this tag is set to the identity of the lex-max observed bidder, so a later bidder with the same value but a higher identity passes the test and is accepted.

Comparison with weak value comparison

Replacing strict $>$ with weak $\ge$ in the acceptance test gives the opposite extreme. Under weak comparison and the equal-value profile $v = (M, M)$ above, both permutations admit the second bidder and deliver welfare $M = \max v$, so this particular failure is avoided.

However, weak comparison is also not constant-competitive: on the needle profile $v = (M, 0, \ldots, 0)$ the observed maximum drops to $0$, and weak comparison admits the first phase-2 arrival unconditionally (every later bidder has value $\ge 0$), giving expected welfare only $(1/n) \cdot M$ (Weak Value Comparison Degrades to 1/n on the Needle Profile). The sample-then-threshold auction's lex rule resolves both failure modes by demanding that the identity also clear an identity tag set from the observed lex-max.

Summary

Acceptance rule Equal-value profile Needle profile Constant competitive?
Strict $p < v$ welfare $= 0$ always (this counterexample) — No
Weak $p \le v$ welfare $= M$ welfare $= M/n$ (Weak Value Comparison Degrades to 1/n on the Needle Profile) No
Lex (price + identity) welfare $= M$ welfare $\ge M/4$ (Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive) Yes

The lex acceptance rule is the unique design among these three that achieves a constant competitive ratio under identity injectivity alone.

Lean formalization

In EconCSLib, the strict variant is the auction Online.Auction.StrictComparison.auction. It is obtained from the generic SingleItemAuction B F template by setting the threshold's identity component to ⊤ : B (under [OrderTop B]). The acceptance condition threshold h ≤ ↑(toLex (v, b)) then degenerates to $p < v$ on first components, since ⊤ ≤ b' fails for every $b' < ⊤$. The counterexample is StrictComparison.welfare_eq_zero: it instantiates $n = 2$, $v = (M, M)$ and computes welfare to be $0$ on both permutations.

The weak variant Online.Auction.WeakComparison.auction is the symmetric specialisation: identity component ⊥ : B (under [OrderBot B]), which makes the test degenerate to $p \le v$ since ⊥ ≤ b' holds for every $b'$. The sample-then-threshold auction Online.Auction.SampleThenThreshold.auction takes neither pole: it sets the identity component to the observed lex-max identity via the same maxPairFold that defines the value threshold.

References

  • [Roughgarden 2016, Lecture 2, Problem 2.1(c)] Tim Roughgarden, Twenty Lectures on Algorithmic Game Theory, Cambridge University Press. Secretary analysis of the online auction (stated for distinct values).
